chunks: Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Abdillah, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdillah, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Daylami, from Ali ibn Ibrahim al-Hashimi who said:

I heard Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him) saying: 'Nothing comes into being except what God has willed, intended, determined, and ordained.' I said: 'What is the meaning of willed?' He said: 'Initiating the act.' I said: 'What is the meaning of determined?' He said: 'Determining the thing in terms of its length and its breadth.' I said: 'What is the meaning of ordained?' He said: 'When He ordains it, He carries it out — and that is what there is no averting.'

key_terms.إرادة: Divine intent — the resolve and decision to act
key_terms.تقدير: Divine determination — the measuring and shaping of a thing in all its dimensions
key_terms.قضاء: Divine ordinance — the final, irrevocable execution of a thing
key_terms.مرد: Averting or turning back — that which cannot be reversed once divine ordinance has been enacted
key_terms.مشيئة: Divine will/desire — the first stage: the initiation of an act

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between divine will, intent, determination, and ordinance in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kadhim (AS) explains to a companion the theological distinctions between four divine attributes: divine will (mashi'ah) as the initiation of an act, divine intent (iradah) as the resolve, divine determination (taqdeer) as the measuring and shaping of a thing in all its dimensions, and divine ordinance (qadha) as the final irrevocable execution. This hadith, from the chapter on desire and intention in Kitab al-Kafi, belongs to the Shia theological tradition of defining these terms precisely to distinguish them from one another, affirming that all things exist only through God's comprehensive governance over creation — from conception to completion.
